title: FOMC Minutes — September 16–17, 2025
html:
Official minutes: HTML · PDF Local PDF: 2025-09-17 FOMC Minutes.pdf

Decision

The Committee cut the federal funds target range by a quarter point to 4 to 4-1/4 percent, the first cut of 2025. Interest on reserve balances fell to 4.15 percent and the primary credit rate to 4.25 percent. The vote was 11-1. Stephen Miran dissented in favor of a half-point cut, citing labor-market softening, underlying inflation he saw as closer to 2 percent, and a lower neutral rate due to tariff revenues and slower population growth. Some participants said holding rates had merit or that they could have supported it, citing stalled inflation progress. Runoff continued at $5 billion (Treasuries) and $35 billion (agency debt and MBS) monthly caps.

Economic outlook

Staff said first-half growth was slower than last year but revised its 2025–2028 GDP projection up somewhat and expected faster growth next year. Participants said growth moderated in the first half, partly on slower consumption, though some saw firming this quarter. Many noted strong high-tech investment, while housing stayed weak and agriculture faced headwinds.

Inflation

August total PCE inflation was estimated at 2.7 percent and core at 2.9 percent, both at the upper end of their 2025 ranges. The statement said "Inflation has moved up and remains somewhat elevated." Staff expected tariffs to lift inflation this year and somewhat in 2026, then a decline to 2 percent in 2027. Participants said longer-term expectations were well anchored; a few said progress had stalled.

Labor market

This was the key shift. Unemployment edged up to 4.3 percent in August. Payroll gains were weak in July and August, and May and June were revised down notably. The BLS preliminary benchmark revision put March 2025 payrolls more than 900,000 below the originally reported level. The vacancies-to-unemployed ratio was 1.0 and average hourly earnings rose 3.7 percent over the year. The statement said the Committee "judges that downside risks to employment have risen."

Financial markets & balance sheet

Treasury yields fell 20 to 40 basis points, most at the short end, steepening the curve. Equities stood near record highs and corporate spreads stayed tight. Repo rates rose, reserves fell sharply on September 15, and standing repo take-up reached $1.5 billion. The deputy manager projected SOMA falling to just over $6 trillion and reserves to about $2.8 trillion by the end of Q1 2026 if runoff continued. Participants said reserves remained abundant but warranted close monitoring.

Risks participants flagged

  • Upside inflation risks: tariff pass-through, persistent inflation and possible upward drift in long-term expectations; a majority emphasized these.
  • Downside employment risks: low hiring and firing, job gains concentrated in a few sectors, rising unemployment for cyclically sensitive groups, possible AI-driven reductions in labor demand and housing weakness.
  • Policy uncertainty on trade, immigration, fiscal spending and regulation.

What it signaled about next moves

Most participants judged it likely appropriate to ease further over the rest of 2025. Some urged caution because financial conditions suggested policy may not be very restrictive. The minutes repeated that "monetary policy was not on a preset course." This was a Summary of Economic Projections meeting, with projections through 2028 released afterward (figures not in the minutes).

Read-through for SPY

  • The start of an easing cycle, with most officials expecting more cuts this year, was a clear tailwind for equities already near record highs.
  • The cut was driven by labor-market weakness, so lower rates came with a softer growth backdrop that could pressure earnings.
  • Some officials' hesitation about cutting with inflation near 2.9 percent core limited how far markets could price an aggressive easing path.
